editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

div1.head: Interview with Mary Louise Jensen Giddens [11/11/2013]

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: My name is Stella Veytsel. We are in Courtroom 304. The court reporter is Cathleen Baker. Our vet is Mary Giddens. She is a civilian who has many stories. Today is November 11, 2013. It's 10:06 a.m., and this is the beginning of the interview. We are in the Lake County courthouse. And let's start with, Mary, so your name is Mary Giddens?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: And what was your maiden name?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Mary Jensen.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: And where were you from?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Waukegan.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: And who did you live with?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: I lived with my parents at the time.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: And when was your date of birth?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: [birth date redacted].

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: Happy birthday. Happy late birthday. So you lived in Waukegan. Do you remember where in Waukegan, like what street, or what part of the city?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: We actually lived in Waukegan when I was first born on the north side; then my parents moved to North Chicago. And I was the second house from a nice big woods that had had all kinds of strawberries, until one day, a fence went up, at World War II. And the fence went up, and there was a boot camp in there. Now, the Navy was segregated at that time, and that camp was black.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: You are kidding.

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: All black.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: How far was that away from your home?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: About one house away. And it was Camp Robert Small, and that was there for a long time. As soon as I was old enough to work weekends and summer vacation in high school, I went and I worked at Camp Green Bay, which was out a ways. And Camp Green Bay had three different canteen buildings. It was huge. And I worked in Number 1311.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: How old were you?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: I started to work in summers at 15 years old, and I stayed there, you know. As soon as I got out of high school, I worked full time. And I scooped ice cream, many, many, many sundaes. And when we got a hundred and something go through, then we'd all give a sigh; and nope, another company's coming, so start over again. After I got full time, I went to the canteen part; and that's when I found the guy that was in the basement, had his office in the basement, was Bill Giddens. And he was the one with the clean clothes that all those guys were wearing. So I finally met him once, and I said -- well, he said, "They are my clothes." So I said, "Thank you," you know, "Nice to know you." And then we went for a long time, I didn't see him. And then I didn't see him around the building at all. He was not coming up very much. He was the bugle master downstairs, in charge of the drum and bugle corp. Then one day, we all went on a picnic, and he was there, at Lake Forest Beach. And we just, "Hi," and that was it. "Hello. How are you?" And then a couple weeks later, a bunch of girls from the neighborhood wanted to go roller stating, and the sailors were going. We all went on the old-fashioned streetcar from right by the Navy base. We walked down there, caught it out to the roller rink Waukegan. One guy said, "I have been here month and haven't seen the lake." So we all took our skates off and walked down to the beach. Well, while we were at the beach, this Bill come up and tapped me on the shoulder and said, very romantically, "You think we could make a go of it?" And I said, "Go of what?" And he said, "Getting married." I said, "Oh, sure. Okay." I thought, "Well, what did I say? He is kidding." Next day, next morning, there he was with rings to match, and that was in the fall. And we were married the 12th of November, 1946, in the Navy chapel, right over by the hospital.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: How many times did you meet him before you married him? How many times did you see him?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Twice. I didn't know him. I didn't even know where he was from. I really didn't.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: What did you think of him when you first saw him?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Well, he was nice looking, and he was polite and always clean-clothed. I don't know. I don't know what I was thinking. I was raised in a very poor neighborhood, and I never went to dances. I finished high school, but I couldn't go to proms or ball games and stuff. And I had to go from North Chicago, take the train to Waukegan, to go to high school, so I didn't have any social activity at all. So I had never -- I didn't know what a date was or a boyfriend or that kind of stuff. So anyway, I found out through the years what he did. And he told me about that he enlisted at 17 in St. Joseph. He was from St. Joseph. He went to Kansas City, and there he went to Farragut, Idaho, for boot camp. And I found out that Farragut property had belonged to Eleanor Roosevelt, and she donated it to the government. And there was a big lake there. He said they needed something that wasn't right on the coast, that wasn't going to be vulnerable in the war. So he was there. That's where they learned that he had played musical instruments in high school, so they got him a bugle and taught him all the bugle calls; and he was a bugle master. Then he went to the west coast and was aboard the USS Steamer Bay. It sailed from Seattle to Honolulu and then right off the coast of Japan. It went to the Philippines, Surigao Strait. They saw Leyte and all, the whole war zone. And I didn't know till I got this paper that there is six battle stars for campaigns in the Pacific. So he didn't talk much about it at first, but through the years, it all came out then. Then he was at Great Lakes for awhile after we were married. Then in 1949, he was sent to Norfolk. And on Norfolk, he was the first active Navy personnel to step aboard this new world's largest cruiser, the USS Newport News. And he had to give the sound for the admiral to take come aboard. And when the admiral came aboard, they gave the admiral the pendant, and he said no. The admiral said no, he was not the first active one; so he gave it to my husband.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: Oh, my God.

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Somebody stole it, so it's gone. He said he was right there, he said, and all of a sudden it was gone. Somebody stole it. But he said the new ship was so good because it didn't have hammocks like the old ship had. And the old ship didn't have air conditioning, so they slept on the deck. He said then, when he got in this new ship, it had air conditioning and bunks. He said it was -- oh. So they sailed out from Norfolk down to Haiti and down the coast of South America and fired off the big guns to let them know how powerful the United States was. Well, his term was up. His enlistment was up. He didn't know whether to reenlist or not, but he found out he would have been sent to Plymouth, England for four years; and he said no. So they said, no, he can't go anywhere else. "That's where you are going to go." So he got out of the Navy and went to barber school. He ended up owning his own barbershop. And then while he was -- during that time, he was elected the first alderman of the new seventh ward in the City of Chicago because it had just been annexed to the city. So he served as an alderman there for 25 years, and he was in charge of building the city hall. Well, the barbershop, the rent went up, and things got too expensive. And he decided that was enough of the barbershop, so he applied for the Lake County Sheriff's Office, and he retired from the Sheriff's office after 20 years.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: Oh, wow. Let me ask you. So you were 15 years old. What makes you want to work at the military?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Well, I am only a house away from the base. I didn't work in Camp Robert Small, but we had an old Nash car. My father was blind, so I drove at 15 years old. But I drove it, so I went out; and Camp Green Bay was not that far away.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: What was Camp Green Bay like?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: It was huge. It actually was -- it was actually like three camps together. I happened to be in one of them. There was 1311 canteen, 1511 canteen and 1711 canteen. And you could see white hats as far as you could see every day, every day, every day, you know, all a field of men. They were men to me. Now they are kids. When I go down there, they are like kids. It was close by. And they even sent me from the canteen, with that old car, they sent me with the money bag from the canteen to bring it over to the bank, so I had to drive the car over there. I didn't think anything of it; had that big bag of money, take it over there, you know. I met a lot of young men. I wrote to a lot of them. A lot of them wrote back. And I don't know what happened to all of those thousands of men.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: When you started there, who would work in the canteen? Were there other women? Were there men working there?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Oh, most of the ship's company -- we were called ship's company, and it was mostly girls and women. We made sundaes and served pie and ice cream and stuff. And then when I got a full-time job, it was behind the counter with candy, gum, cigarettes and, you know, stuff like that, and right next to the drill hall. In the winter, they paraded in the drill hall.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: What did they do? So when they have this camp, what do they do there? Is this where they train?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: This is where they trained. It's boot camp. They trained them. They marched an awful lot. Then, I guess, some of them went to the rifle range, and then they kind of sorted out what you are going to be. Are you going to be a cook? What are you going to be? What suits your talent?

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: Did you find that you became close to these women? Did you make friends?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Oh, sure. You know, that's the ones that some went roller skating and some from the neighborhood did. We got together for years. Then, of course, most of them married off and went off over here and there and wherever. One of them that worked for my husband in the drum and bugle corp still lives in Kenosha, and I hear and see them all the time. They are still close friends. It's been quite a life. We traveled a lot. We camped, mostly camped, from coast to coast. I still go down to the base with the VFW. We take pie and ice cream down there. Of course, our big do of the year is the sailor party about two weeks before Christmas, the guys that aren't going home, and the girls now, too. I wanted to be one, but they wouldn't take girls then. So now, at Christmastime, we serve anywhere from 120 on up, and down to 100, 120 sailors at a time. And we pack a little bag ahead, the night before, that we are going to give them when they go back with goodies in it, and then they have an absolute, full dinner, buffet style, all they want. You can have seconds. But they are like little kids. We don't put the dessert out until after they eat. Then after they all had gone through the line, we bring out tables and tables of dessert. We have entertainment called The Little People, with big costumes and everything; they come in. And then we have -- one of our women is a professional singer. She leads them in song. Then they clear the tables back, and they can dance. And then they can come back and eat whatever they want, as much as they want. They can eat all evening. If they don't want to dance, we have games laying on the tables. And we have school buses that pick them up. Our drivers go down and get them from the base, bringing them up in school buses. When they go back down to go back, then I hand them all -- it's always my job to hand them this little, like, a lunch bag with candy and gum and a deck of cards in it. And that's our big deal.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: Do you feel like because you spent almost all of your life, from when you were 15, do you feel like the military is family?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Oh, yeah. And, of course, you have to make fun of the other. If you are one division, you would make fun of the other. You know, when you see a Marine, you go "Yee haw" and, you know. But I enjoyed every minute of it. I have to say, it was a different experience.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: Did you want to -- were you ever thinking about, to yourself, like, "I want to join the military"?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: I wanted to when I was old enough, but they didn't take girls. No women. Women were called Waves. I have a friend that was a Wave for over 20 years, but she never -- They were Navy, but not regular Navy. They were called Waves. In fact, the day we got married, he was late for the ceremony because he went to pick up his leave papers, 30-day leave, and a Wave had lost them. So he had to go to the captain, and the captain gave him a 10-day emergency leave. That's why he was late. I am standing in the chapel saying, "He's not coming." But he came with the papers in his hand and an orchid corsage in the other hand. Of course, I couldn't have a wedding gown. I couldn't afford it. We went and had cake and coffee at my mother-and-dad's. We got in the Nash, and we drove to his mother's in St. Joe, Missouri. There were no interstates then. It took us all night to get to his mother's. We got there about 8:00 o'clock, 9:00 o'clock the next morning; and then I met his family.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: So when you were there, before you ever met Bill, did you feel like all the men were enjoying having the women there? They liked no flirt with you?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Oh, sure, sure. Of course, by the time I was 17, you know, I am thinking, you know, all these guys are winking at me and that, and I thought, "This is great. Look at all these men." Now I go down and say, "Look at all those kids." But I go down there, like I say, once a month for that; and then I go for -- they have the sailor party. And then we have a veterans party, a veterans dinner. I think that's coming up next week, a veterans dinner. Ride in the parades.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: Did you find that when you were there and the men, would they talk to you, would they share with you their fears; or how would they treat you?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: You mean now?

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: No. When you were there when you were 17, 15, 19.

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Oh, yeah. A lot of them were anxious to tell you. They would tell me where they were from, you know. Some of them said, "Well, we didn't want to end up being drafted" and stuff like that. So it was a nice experience. And I heard so much about what they did and where they lived, you know. And a lot of them, they wanted an address, so I gave them my address. And I'd get letters from them, and I'd answer them. It went on for two or three years, I'd hear from some of those guys.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: How many letters do you think you would write in a year?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Oh, I don't know, 18, 20. It would depend on who wrote to me, and I would answer, just because they had written to me. And I figured, well, the poor guy, and what ship they are on and where they are at. I have often wondered what happened to all those guys.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: So when you met Bill, how old were you? Were you 19 or 20?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: I was 19. I didn't turn 20 till the 26th of October, and so I was 20 when I got married. Bill was 21.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: Now, so when you married him, you said you weren't able to afford a dress. So what did you do? Do you remember what you wore?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Yeah. I had a very, what's called powder green light suit I bought for Easter and a white blouse. Of course he gave me an orchid corsage, which, incidentally, is still pressed in a bible in the cedar chest. Of course, he had his dress uniform, which was fine. And my mother and father were there. My brother and his sister-in-law stood up for us. My mother was almost ready to faint. But then he had two or three Navy buddies, and that was it.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: When he was shipped, did he get shipped overseas pretty quickly after your marriage?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Oh, he had been overseas before we were married. He had been in the South Pacific before I knew him. But then he was shipped to -- we were married about, almost three years before they sent him to Norfolk. And I went out there, but there was nothing. No place to go, nothing. People say there is no signs on the grass. There were signs on the grass. "Sailors and dogs, stay off the grass." People said that wasn't true. I said, "I saw it. I was there." I had a sleeping room there. I was there for almost two months. What am I going to do? So I drove back home until he got out.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: So when you were married to him and he was in the war or out overseas, what did you do? Did you still work at the canteen?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I still worked there. I worked practically till well up in the fifties. And then I worked at a grocery store, which paid a lot more then; and I worked for three different grocery companies, until I retired from them. And so all together, it was a long time, but it doesn't seem like it now. It seemed like it just went poof, you know?

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: Did you have a uniform?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: We had a uniform all right, a Mother Hubbard thing that tied around you, one size fits all. No matter how big or how little you were, that was it. But we had to wear that in the canteen and that. At the grocery store, we still had smocks and stuff. And he always did his own laundry. I never did that. That was something else that he said was, on the old Steamer Bay, they washed their clothes in a bucket of saltwater and hung them on a rope on the ship. When he got to the Newport News, they had a laundry; so that was class for him.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: So when you were in the canteen, did you have to do the men's laundry, or would they ask you?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: No. No. No. No. We didn't handle anything like that. We just sold the stuff to them. They came in, you know. And when they came in, the whole company, they would line all up. And the funny thing about -- I always give this speech at the Christmas party. Do you know about the Navy's flying five? Well, you know, there are some planes out in Lake Michigan still down on the bottom. I say, "I am not talking about airplanes." The flying five -- the paymaster would set up his table, and the men would come into the drill hall, line up and get their first Navy pay, seven dollars. They'd get a five-dollar bill and a two-dollar bill. Then they go past us in the canteen, and we had to give them their toiletry kit. It had everything in it you could imagine. And at first, it used to have a bottle of aftershave, until they found out there was a lot of alcohol in aftershave, and more was going in the mouth instead of on the outside of the cheeks, so they took that out. Then they came to the end of the line with this in their hand. They had to pay the canteen five dollars. It was the flying five. It flew from the paymaster to the canteen. That left them with two dollars. Well, my husband through the years collected two-dollar bills around the area. All the businesses in town had two-dollar bills. So there is a wad of them yet in the cedar chest. So every Christmas when I give this little speech at the end, I always ask the guys at the base that put this together to come forward, and I usually have something that I bought personally that I bought for them, like a pin or a T-shirt, not from the VFW, from me. And I said, "Here is one of those two-dollar bills from World War II." So I have been handing those out one at a time every year.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: That's amazing. How much would ice cream cost? So what would they do with their two dollars?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: The two dollars -- I don't know what they were charging then. First when they were in boot camp, they didn't pay anything. They just came through the line. It was like a chow line. We made the sundaes and piled them out on the counter, and they just went through the line. Of course, when you got away from being in boot camp, then, of course, they paid for it in the canteen.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: They must have loved the ice cream. That must have been their favorite part.

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: The last I worked on the base was in the photo lab in the basement of the Hostess House. And when I came back from that late from the wedding, I was developing some film, and I thought, "This looks awfully familiar." I said, "That's got to be -- look at the flowers." I said, "That's got to be the chapel." I looked at the date on the back. It was the afternoon that I had got married in the morning. That was the picture taken in the afternoon. No wonder all those flowers were there. It was the captain's daughter's wedding in the afternoon. I said, "Well, she got secondhand flowers." I was there in the morning. I thought that was pretty nice.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: It was pretty and made up?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: It was beautiful. "Look at all these flowers." I just happened. Of course, we had that shortened days. By the time I got down there developing these pictures, it looked familiar. She said it was captain's daughter gotten married. I still remember our chaplain was Chaplain Kaberle. I can remember that like yesterday. But where is my car keys? I don't know.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: Not as important.

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: No. No.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: What about, like, your parents? You said your dad went blind or was blind?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: He went blind during when I was about a teenager. He lost his sight completely. And my mother was deaf from day one. So my childhood was kind of -- that's why I didn't get partying and boyfriends or anything, because he is going blind and she is deaf; and I had to communicate between the two of them.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: So did you know sign language, or how did you communicate with your mom?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Well, her, she, you know, she could see. She could read, and she could see and everything. I'd motion to her. But then, of course, my dad, I'd have to tell him and read if it's something he needed to sign or something, you know. That's why I drove so early. I was only 15. Didn't bother with a driver's license. Sat on two pillows.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: How did you learn? Where did you learn to drive?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: The neighbor across the alley took me out, and they drove me out, took me. I drove downtown to downtown North Chicago, and somebody else was down there. My dad and this other guy met, and they decided they wanted to go someplace; and, "Here. Here's the keys. Drive home." A big shot. I thought, "Oh, boy." I drove home all by myself. I don't know. I look back; I don't know how we did it.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: Did you think that when the camp started going up, did that change the neighborhood? Did that change things?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Where Camp Robert Smalls was is now Navy housing. All three of those camps on Green Bay are all Navy housing, too. The VA Hospital, when I went to grade school, was across the street from me, from the school. Sometimes they would have World War I guys out working in the garden, and they would wander over to see. They didn't hurt anything, but kids playing recess, and they would come over. And the teacher would have to call, "Your guys are over here." They would come and get them. Didn't have to worry anything was going to happen in those days. So, the school was there. And that one building was across the street. That's the Navy hospital. When I go down there now, I can't believe how many buildings there are. And I went with the Christmas Cheer, and they had a wheelchair for me. I said, "I don't need a wheelchair." So our Santa Claus plopped himself in the wheelchair, and we pushed him. We went from building to building. There is tunnels underneath, concrete tunnels, from one building to the other. We don't go outside. You go in one building; you can go to the next building without going outside. You come up an elevator in the next building. So we went singing Christmas carols from one to another under the basement.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: Do you remember when the tunnels were created?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: That's what they got now. They made those when they got so many buildings because people were going to have to go outside. What if you had to take a wheelchair to another place? So it's a big tunnel. And you would go down in the tunnel and walk up, you were going to come up in that building. And we had a map of where we supposed to sing. So Santa Claus rode in the wheelchair, and I walked.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: Nice Santa Claus. Sounds wonderful. What about when you were done with part-time and you started full-time? Did you still serve ice cream?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: No. No. I ended up, as soon as I was that far up the ladder, so to speak, I was working in the canteen and, you know, cigarettes and stuff like that. And the guys would come through in a line. And during the day, the ship's company men could come in any time of the day. If they had an office in the building, they could come in and buy something any time they wanted to. But the recruits came in in lines.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: How much was everything? How much were cigarettes back then?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Oh, God. I don't know. Probably not more than 20 or 25 cents. Like gasoline was 15 cents, 13 cents. It was quite -- but then, you figure what I was earning. When I first started there, I got 25 cents an hour. Then when I went to the canteen, I got 50 cents an hour. That was double wages, so that was quit a bit for me. But I helped out at home. I ended up buying a new stove for my mother and an easy chair for my dad. I mean, because I figured, it was something they couldn't afford, so it was nice.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: Did you live with them once you got married?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: No. No. No. We couldn't get an apartment. They were very, oh, when they depended on the Navy for the money, they didn't want to rent to you. We had in the course of time four different sleeping rooms. That was it, you know. And, of course, he could eat at the base; but I had to eat -- I ate a lot of meals in the dime store and little restaurants down by 22nd Street right by the Navy gate. Our big night out on Friday night was to go on those hamburger joints over near the Waukegan High School because when I went to high school, I carried my lunch. But this was a big deal. Friday night we had a hamburger at one of those places by the W shop or something.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: Would you go with other Navy guys?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Oh, some of them. Like I say, the one that lives in Kenosha now, he was from Pennsylvania. And so he brought his bride from there that they went to high school together. And when they were married, they live right up here in Kenosha now. We see them quite often. Once in awhile we would hear from somebody. World War II veterans are getting a little scarce now.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: What about when you guys were married and he was away from home? Would you write letters to each other?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Yeah. And one time I drove out by myself from here, from Great Lakes out to Virginia; and he managed to have a sleeping room set up for us. But I got out there. He said, "Now call this number. It will be to the ship." I gave the number, and the voice said, "Mary Lou, I know you." I said, "You do?" He said, "Yeah." He said, "When I was in boot camp, I remember you worked in the canteen." Here was a guy on the ship answering the phone. I had no idea who he was. He knew, when he heard my name, he said, "I know who you are." So then he talked to Bill, and he came down the gangplank with a patch over one eye; and I said, "What happened?" He said, "Well, somebody threw something," and it hit him in the eye. So he had a big black monocle, big black patch on his eye. And then later on, we went out. He was going on leave. My sister-in-law went with me. We went out there and picked him up. And he said, "Let's go up to the Statue of Liberty and go to New York City and drive back home." So that was it.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: How long did it take you to drive to Virginia? Forever? Hours and hours and hours, right?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Well, the first time I drove out, I drove as far as someplace in Ohio that was a wife of one of the sailors. I was supposed to pick her up. Well, she didn't drive, so I stayed with her overnight, and we drove out. By that time, we had a brand new '48 Studebaker, blue. And we stayed in this hotel, and they parked it up on the roof with a number on the window. And I come in the morning to get it. "Where is my car?" And they said, "Oh, it's here. This is your car." I said, "This isn't my car. This is a Plymouth. I don't own a Plymouth." He said, "It's your number on the window." I said, "I don't care what number it is. That's not my car." So I had to go up on the roof and say, "There is my car, that Studebaker. I know it's mine. Here is my ID card." "Oh. Well, I don't know how this happened. It got mixed up." They were so sorry. Well, I found out after I got back home later, and a knock on the door, FBI. "Did anything ever happen very funny when were you in Virginia in hotel?" I said, "Yeah." I told him. He said, "Oh, that explains a lot." I said, "Explains a lot of what?" He said, "There was a murder in the hotel, and they took the body out and dumped it." And he said, "They must have grabbed your car; and they got the numbers mixed up, and your car had a number for that Plymouth that was the other guy's."

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: Oh, my God.

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: That scared the life out of me. My car had a dead body in it?

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: What year was this?

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: Oh, my gosh.

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: I said, "What? The FBI at the door? What did I do," you know?

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Lots of interesting things, you know, through the years, this and that happening here and there. Bill came down with malaria, and I took him to the hospital. And I called in the morning and I wanted to know how he was; and they said, "Oh, his strep throat's doing better." I said, "He didn't go in with strep throat. He's got malaria." I thought, okay oh, another mistake. Good grief. A short time after that, his hands were itching and the skin was coming off. We took him to Hines Hospital. Hines couldn't take care of him. But the Navy had a research hospital right in Chicago, right on the lake. Northwestern has it now, but it was right on the lake. And they took him in there, and they called it -- he said he knew what it was. He said, "I remember the guys were all having itchy hands when we came back from that one island where we had to deliver food. We delivered food, and the natives were all scratching." He said, "We caught something, and it went away." But his broke out later and was so bad, his fingernails fell off. And he said he was screaming in pain. He said they put some solution around his hands and put plastic bags over his hands, and he said that didn't help. He said they caught him in the bathroom one night with the red hot water in the bathroom on his hands to stop the itching. He was there. We weren't married very long, and I was going back and forth to Chicago on my day off on Sunday. And finally -- he was there eleven-and-a-half months. And when he came home, he had a stack like that of papers and end top, "diagnosis unknown."

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: Oh, my God.

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Navy research.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: Well done.

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Well done.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: And what year was that? How old was he?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Well, let's see. He was from '25 to '49. Is that 30 something? He was still a young man, but he said, "I broke out." A couple times during that time in between it was kind of itchy, and he put something on it. But that time it was absolutely berserk. The fingernails fell out or something. And he said, "Here was the papers. Diagnosis unknown."

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: And you said what he was, a bugle master? What's a bugle master?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Well, there was a call for everything, chow call, Taps, reveille. There was a certain call for everything you wanted to have done. He had to know them all because if you were over here and that was just for you, you knew what you were supposed to listen for, because there were not these electronic communications on the ship. That was it. You stood up there, like here, stand there and give the sign what the guys are supposed to do or where they are going and all that kind of stuff. You had to be able to transmit that by the bugle sounds.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: So once he learned that, he was on a ship doing that?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Yes, right here.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: What years did he do that, or do you remember what months or what years?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: That was -- well, after he left, right after he left here -- he was here in '42. Must have been '43 until '45, at least late '45, before he came back from South Pacific.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: And that was before you guys got married, or was that after?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: That was before. Yeah, that was before. I didn't know him till he came to Great Lakes. So this and this. This is up on the bridge of the Steamer Bay, and that's the Steamer Bay, and I think this one is -- This is the Newport News.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: So where did he go once you guys got married?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Well, we were at the base. Then he went to Norfolk.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: What was he doing there, and how long?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Well, he was bugle master on that, too, but they didn't have as many sounds because they were beginning to have electronic equipment. He was gone for quite awhile. Like I say, they went down to Haiti and down the coast of South America. He was gone for six or seven months at least. And then his time was up for him to reenlist, and he didn't want to go to England.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: What was it like for you to be married to somebody who was in the Navy who was overseas?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Well, I was busy working. And we finally did get a little one-bedroom house later on, after about three or four different. And then, of course, after he got out of the Navy, or while he was still in the Navy, actually, and during the time he was getting out, after he came home, he built a house.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: Oh, my gosh.

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: He did everything himself, except the cabinets. We had a good life. And he served the City of North Chicago for 25 years, and then here for 20 years.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: He had an illustrious career. Amazing.

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: The stories at the courthouse, too. He was with Judge Homer, Judge Ingalls. I don't know who all. He just puttered around all over the place. He even went down to Tennessee to bring a prisoner back, a prisoner who happened to be a brother of the girl I worked with. That was embarrassing as heck. He had skipped out on his -- His mother put her house up as a bond. When he left, mother lost the house. And she is working with me, and I know all this; and I don't want to say anything to the other girls because Bill it is telling me all this. He went down with another guy, brought the guy back. He didn't give him a hard time at all. He said he just brought him back, and here you are.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: Did you find that because you were the wife of a Navy -- Does that change things for you? Did people treatment you differently in the canteen, or did people treat you differently here?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: No, they didn't treat me differently. Well, I was pretty busy. But, like I say, you know, Waukegan and this area depended on the Navy a lot; but they treated them kind of, you know, there is a bunch of sailors and that. To me, I was so used to Navy, you know? And even the black guys -- don't put this in there. At night when the guys are on guard duty, they are so black you can see the little hats going down the side of the fence. They'd holler, "Hi." I would say, "Hi." People said, "They were segregated?" I said, "Yeah." Some of my friends say, when I said that Camp Robert Small was at the end of my street, they said, "There is no Camp Robert Small." I said, "No, not now." There is Dewey, Perry, Porter. There is not Camp Green Bay. There is a lot of camps down there yet.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: How did people react when the camp was built in the first place, the one that was right next to you?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Well, we missed out on our pond we used to skate on. My mother and I used to go and get raspberries and strawberries, and she canned them all the time; and we had rows and rows of them in the fruit cellar. All of a sudden, this big metal fence went up, and they were parading around, and they were all black. Of course, now it's not segregated. Of course, my ambition, living right by the Navy base, I wanted to join Navy. But I wore glasses, and that was a no-no. And I was a girl. That was a no-no. So I did the next best thing, ship's company.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: You said "ship's company." What exactly -- how does one apply for that?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: You apply -- you worked for the Navy. And they had canteens, and the photo lab was run by them. And I guess they must still call them ship's company because they are -- you work for the Navy, but you are not Navy.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: You said something like a WFO maybe or that you guys are called something when you throw the parties now for the Navy. Were the women called something? Was there a name for the women?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Like the party? We are all VFW members. We were the auxiliary.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: And what's that mean, "VFW members"?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: "VFW" means Veteran of Foreign Wars. Any service personnel that served in a war zone can join that. Now, it's not like the other branches of American Legion. They don't have to be in a foreign war zone. But VFW have to have been in a war zone. Then the wives can join the auxiliary. That's what I am in. I am a life member of the auxiliary. Now, we have one of our women in our auxiliary who spent 21 years in the regular Navy. But she can't join the VFW part because she was never in a war zone; but her father was, so she could apply for the auxiliary. But with her overseas in Morocco, that was not a war zone. She said they brought the wounded in, and she tended to the wounded over there, but she said she was not in the war zone. You had to be a veteran of foreign wars.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: That makes sense.

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: We are right up in Winthrop Harbor.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: And you guys still throw all those events for the Navy?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Oh, yeah. And we have a veterans dinner and, you know, that breakfast where they have a big breakfast. I usually work that. We have a bake sale. We just had a craft show, and we worked that and made some money off of that; and that all goes to our fund for mailing. We mail boxes overseas; and the postage, you know, is pretty hefty. We have to put toothbrushes and magazines and puzzles and all kinds of stuff in the box. There are certain things you can't put in, but we pack those boxes and ship them overseas.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: That's so kind. That's amazing.

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Just tell them, you know, if you know somebody overseas, give us a name; and we will send it to them, and they could pass it out. At one time, the women got together up there in the kitchen to bake cookies, a hundred dozen cookies, packed them very carefully in separate boxes and sent them over there. We got three or four letters back. One guy, when he came back on leave, came to the post because he wanted to talk to the auxiliary. He said he had to pass those cookies out one to a guy because he said they were just lined up for homemade cookies, you know. He said they just lined up. He said, "One cookie." He said that they got to the end of the line and came through again. That was okay, but he couldn't give them two or three because he didn't know how many cookies he had. We baked cookies, and we sent other stuff. Takes up all my time, but that's good. Of course, I got the civilian job of president of a women's club, too.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: What's that?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Well, it's a women's club, originally North Chicago. It's still called that, but there is hardly anybody from North Chicago in it. And this week Wednesday we go to shop to fill 25 Christmas stockings for little girls four and five years old. One time it went to Catholic Charities. This time, it's going to go to the Salvation Army for their Christmas party.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: When did you join that?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Oh, God. I have been in that for 30 years. I have been president about the last six or seven years. Every time there's a reelection, it's, "You are doing a good job. We don't need a vote." I don't want the secretary/treasurer job. That's a bigger job. Like I said, we met last week, and we are going to shop next week; and we have to have this all ready to go. We have our Christmas party. We bring out all the stuff that we bought and pass the stocking down, and everybody take it off their box and fill the stocking; and then they put the stockings. Guess who gets to take them down?

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: You are so busy.

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: And one time, it was a snowstorm, and the party was in Pleasant Prairie, right up here. And we got all the stuff put together and put it in boxes; and I was in the Jeep, and it was full. I mean the boxes, it was just me and the boxes; and it was snowing like mad. I thought, "Please don't let me have an accident. They are going to say, 'Mrs. Santa Claus had an accident and lost all the presents.'" When I got down there, I said, "Take all the boxes." I didn't care if I got in an accident on the way home. "Take all your stuff." I got that coming up in the next month. I'll go shopping at The Dollar Store.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: Can I ask you a question about this picture? It's the one that looks like they are marching in an event. Did you ever get to see that?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: This is Ross Field down on the base. This is Ross Field at the base down here at Great Lakes. And they have a review every Saturday. Every Saturday they had to do this. At every graduation, they still do this. For every graduation, when a company graduates, they have this to lead them. They lead the procession, and they play the music and everything in Ross Field. And then, also, the bugle master has to assign somebody to sound reveille in the morning, and Taps, and then evening colors. Now, you have the raising of the flag. There is a call for that. Of course, we live so close, I could hear it every day. And you could hear it that he did it a lot of times. And then in the evening, and then, oh, a lot of big bands would come to play. And Bill, he used to say, "Well, the big bands came here to listen to me." Then they would have a movie. He liked to take the evening colors because we would be there afterwards. We could go into the building where they have the free movie, and we could see the movie. This is Ross Field in Great Lakes.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: And that was in 1946?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: In May?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Navy day in 1946. This was before we were married.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: Did you get to see the procession?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Oh, I used to see a lot of this, yes. Sometimes when there was a movie in the drill hall for the recruits, Bill would say, "You want to come down?" I would say, "Sure." We'd go inside there. We had a little puppy, and we let the puppy loose; and the guys just loved it. The puppy would run all around, and they'd pet it. It was fun, you know? I enjoyed every minute of it. I can't say I enjoyed it when he was gone. He was safe. He said he didn't get ever shot. He said he had it around him. He said one of the guys backed up into an airplane prop, and he said that was kind of a disaster. But he said he had sounded over a hundred funerals, so he always said, "When I go, I want Taps." So he went in August of 2010, and the VFW had their service, and they had Taps. And then we when we got to the cemetery, we had a military funeral. And for me, it was odd to see a girl and a guy on each end of the thing. And I know that that young guy didn't know us from Adam, but he stood at attention and had tears in his eyes. Then we came in the chapel, and they had their military service, and we heard Taps. And then they folded the flag, and then he handed it to her. She handed it back to him, and then they came over and handed it to me. Now, that's a tearjerker, when they hand you the flag. I said, "I don't want to go over to the grave now." So he is buried down near North Chicago in the cemetery down there.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: And what was his date of birth?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: August 3, 1925.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: And what was his full name?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: William Jessie Giddens. Jessie comes from Jessie James from St. Joseph, Missouri. There is a house there belonged to Jessie James. Everybody in his family was William or Jessie, Jessie William or William Jessie. And I was Mary. His mother was Mary. My mother was Mary. I had a cousin Mary. He had a cousin Mary. He was surrounded by Marys. So they all called me Mary Lou because you had to designate which Mary they are talking about. I was Mary Lou. His mother was Mary Jane. I chatter on too much. I am used to being alone; and when I get out, I want to talk all the time.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: No. This is wonderful. What about, did he -- was he ever -- you said something about medals or special awards for him.

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Here.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: So what about, did you get to see any of his awards being given to him or handed to him?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: No. They were always done either on the base or on the ship. I don't know one from another, but there is a great big thing in the basement like this with all his medals. Plus, he was a volunteer fireman, he was an alderman 25 years, and then he was a deputy sheriff. So all those badges are down in the bottom there. But all these ribbons, I suppose a guy in the service would know. But I don't know what, when you see something like this -- He never told me that he had been in six battles, six battle stars. And I thought, "He never told me that." I found this down in the bottom when I was cleaning out his desk.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: What about, what is that, combat action, number six?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Yeah, because there was action from his ship. This was in the zone, in the zone where the battles are, right in the zone. But this is actually when his ship was actually in battle. So he got a Battlestar for that being in the action. Then he went to Great Lakes, and all the other was -- this was like -- I don't know. Like, we called it cold war stuff. This here was all to show off the ship. And he got this medal from '43 to '54, but he was in -- service commemorative medals and all of that. I don't know -- when I see them on the board, I don't know what they are.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: You said he went to Hawaii, too?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: He went to Hawaii first. That's why the picture there was the first -- when he left Seattle, the ship stopped in Hawaii. He said that was when, on that Hawaii beach, there was one hotel. I was there last October. You couldn't walk between them. The Waikiki beach is a disaster. I wanted to go on board on the Arizona. Of course, when you are on a tour, you have to go with. We made all four islands. But when we went to Pearl Harbor, we went aboard the Arizona, and you cross on a platform. They said oil still comes bubbling up. There are thousands of men still down there. But they said they did not drown. They burned first. That's why they didn't even try to get them out, because it burned inside before it sank. And they said all those thousands of bodies are still down there. They were burned, and then they were filled with water. So once in awhile, they say, a bubble of oil still comes up. I wanted to see more, but then the tour bus, you got to get back on. That was the only reason I went to Hawaii. It was not the hula dancers and all that. I happened to be there for my birthday. The guide we had, my friend I was with, her and her husband, they told the guide, "Oh, birthday cake." Oh, everybody's clapping. Another island; birthday cake. Happy birthday. Island three, happy birthday. Island four was when they had the luau with all kinds of people, thousands of people with torches and everything. Come down the middle of the aisle, a great big torch and somebody carrying a birthday cake. I had four birthday cakes. I thought, "Oh, my."

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: No more birthday cake?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Yeah. It was fun.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: Was your husband ever in Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Oh, yeah. That's where that was. But he was there after Pearl Harbor had been hit because, see, Pearl Harbor was '41; and he wasn't 17 until '42. So he joined when three or four of his cousins joined. And the twins, his cousins, when they went down, they were there. His one cousin, Willie, was too little; and he didn't weigh enough, so they told him, "Eat a lot of bananas." So Willie stuffed himself with bananas. He gained four pounds, but he didn't end up getting in. But Willie served very well as a civilian, because he went to work in an airplane factory. He was little. He could crawl in and out. So I said, I think he did as much as the guys in the service, but he just couldn't be in the service.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: Too little?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Yeah, too little. He said he had a lot of souvenirs in a box, and some guy was getting shipped home, and so he said he'd take it home for him. He never saw the box again. Of course, I have a grass skirt, and it's in the cedar chest, that he had brought back. And when he went to Haiti, I have a big box carved, hand-carved box from Haiti. While he was in the Philippines, he talked to the guys there, and he said they took him out in the jungle and showed some of the slaughter out in the jungle that the Japanese had done. And he said those little Filipinos were tough little fighters. So he said, "I want to show you." He had a box. It had a knife. Up by the handle was very narrow, and then it spread out, and it was about this long. And I said, "What do you do with that?" He said, "It belonged to that guy." I said, "It's old? He said, "Yeah. He used it." I said, "What's it for?" He said, "What do you think? Why do you think it's narrow there?" {Indicating} "That's what those little Filipinos did. He said that's what that knife was for, narrow to hit the Jap in the neck. The Japs did worse that than that to our guys. Bill said those guys were telling him what they found in the jungle where the Japanese had been because he said it was -- I can't even tell you what they did to our guys. And, but when he landed in this little village in the Philippines, he said, "No women; no children." He said, "They are up in the hills." He said, "They don't know who this is that landed. They are hiding up there. They don't know if it's Japanese or Americans." They had to signal to them that it was safe to come down. So when they came down, he said they were ragged and everything. The guys were giving them their t-shirts and their socks and everything and whatever they could take off to give them to wear because their clothes were all ripped up. They had been up there, hiding from the Japanese. He didn't tell me all that stuff right at first. Through the years little things would come up, and he'd tell me about it. But that knife kind of scared me. But so, that's my history, his history, of World War II.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: Well, your history and his history is amazing. Thank you so much for sharing it with us. I know it's just about your everyday, but for us --

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Every day I think of some little thing and, oh, yeah, yeah, okay. You know, I hear these names up here at the courthouse and that. I should have brought this picture up that's on Bill's wall in his room. It's Fred Foreman's big campaign picture that he had out when he was running, first running for state's attorney, because Bill knew him when he was just a lawyer in somebody's office, you know? And Fred came to his funeral. I had such an, oh, God, such a big funeral. I didn't want to have a night before and funeral. I said, that's too much. I don't think I could take that. Well, the morning will be enough. And it was supposed to be from 11:00 to 2:00. I got there at 10:30; there was a line already. And the people I didn't know and came from -- of course, he was also a Mason, a Mason and a Shriner and belonged to the Valley of Chicago. It's a little step up from a regular Mason. And he was 32-degree Mason. He was stepped over to that. Then he joined the Tebala Shrine out in Rockford. Then Waukegan has the Tebala Motor Patrol. You probably see them riding the motorcycles in the parades. Well, he did that, too. That was another hobby, like. That's the one they all came in their aprons, and we had the Masonic funeral. We had the Masonic funeral. We had the VFW funeral. We had the Navy funeral. He had the whole works.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: Out of curiosity, did you see the boot camp training, all those guys getting trained, when you were at the canteen?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Oh, sure. I could look right out the window. In that little restaurant, we'd change clothes in the back. I could peek out and see all those guys out there. Look at all those men. Now I look at all those kids. But oh, yeah, I could see them training. When they were marching, you could tell, you know. They had music. They had a band. There were actually three camps on Green Bay. Then there was Dewey, Perry, Moffett and then, of course, Camp Robert Small. It was all over the place. It just popped like overnight because our berry patch was gone, and our pond was gone.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: Did it change everything around the area, too?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Oh, yeah. You know, everybody that had an extra room was renting it out to people like me. First one I had was down off of Tenth Street in Waukegan, until I woke up one morning, and the little kid and the whole family is standing at the food of the bed, "Good morning." I said, "That's all." So we moved up in Waukegan off Grand Avenue. We had a sleeping room on Buttrick Street. We'd look in the paper for one that's closer to the base. One, we had to park the car a block away in the wintertime. And finally, we got to rent this little one-room house in North Chicago. We started from there. He built a two-bedroom house. He built it himself. Then we bought a house west of Green Bay Road, and we lived there for 20 years, '62 to '82. And in '82 we moved over to Beach Park.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: Was it weird or different when you are married and you just met the guy? How was it to get to know him while you are married?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Well, I asked him all about what he did, and we just talked about what we did and about our relatives and about his farm. We went down one time to visit his cousin on a farm one time. And it was harvest time, and she was a young bride. She was about 20 years old, too. They had all these people come to help, and they had all this food spread out, and all those harvesters come and eat, you know? I thought, "Oh, I am glad I didn't marry him. I couldn't have done that." But it was interesting. And I never ate so many beans in my life. Every meal. Every meal the bowl of beans was in the middle of the table. No matter where we went, what time of day, there is the beans. And he liked beans; and he said, in the Navy, Wednesday was always beans. Did you ever notice restaurants do that now? They always have bean soup on Wednesday. And he said he liked it. They had beans for breakfast. Sometimes in the chow line, he said, the guys, "ahhh." He said he liked it. The other guys didn't want to eat those beans for breakfast. But one little incident that's kind of nasty. They had a pile of spaghetti and rice on the deck of that Steamer Bay. And he said, of course, the guys knew it was going to the Japanese prison camp. So you know what they did to it when they went by it? They wet on it and everything because it's going to go to those damn Japs, you know? He said he would see the guys doing that all the time. Well, they got paid back for that. Their supply ship was sunk. What is the cook going to serve? Rice and spaghetti. You know, to his dying day, he would not eat either one. He did not even want it on the table. He would say, "I can still see it moving." He said, in the hot sun, it smelled terrible. That poor cook. What's he going to do? He had to wash it the best he could, clean it up. To his dying day, he never would touch spaghetti or rice. Little things the guys did. They hated them, hated them, hated them, you know. But he had one incident on a plane. There was a photo book. So they asked him if he would sit in the gun turret, and this other guy from Texas was going to pilot, and he said Bill should take some pictures. And he said he took those pictures, and he said, "Hey, we hit the ground." And he said, "That stupid Texan." They hit the ground and flew up. He had landed on Iwo Jima, and he said he went "pfft." And he said afterwards, when he found out the story of Iwo Jima, he said, "I can't believe this." He said, "That stupid Texan. We got back riddled with holes." He said, he never told him how come they got riddled with holes. He said, they just shot them because they saw them in the air. Little stories. It didn't come out right away; through the years. I said, "What happened to that Texan?" He said, "Nothing. He didn't know he did that because he just --" He said, "We just 'pfft.'" And he says, "What?" But it was interesting. So many things happened, and so many of them, like he said, that ship next to him was sunk, and his cousins were sunk. He said that the worst part when that next ship was sunk, they had to all go out there and try and find bodies and body parts and stuff like that. He said, those two little ships were not very big. He said, it went down -- that one went down like -- He said, "Twenty minutes sooner, it would have been me." But it wasn't to be. CATHLEEN BAKER: Can I interrupt for a second? When we were off the record earlier, you told us something about what they found about the Japanese plane on that ship. I thought that was pretty interesting. You might want to ask about that.

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Well, the plane was in good enough shape for them to see it. And he said, that story about the white scarves and do it for the emperor, he said, they didn't have any landing gear on those planes, and they were shackled to the floor.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: So who was this?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Those Kamikazes, they were not volunteering for the glory. Maybe the first few for the glory of the emperor with the white scarves. But they were taught how to fly, but not -- they didn't have to land because there was no landing gear. You go find the ship, and that's it.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: So they found a ship, and he saw that they had no landing gear?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: They saw -- when all this is sinking around him, but they got the plane. They got to look in the plane. The plane was still sitting kind of on top, and it was burned a little. But he said there was shackles on the ankles and no landing gear. He said, they couldn't have flown off somewhere if they wanted to because where are they going to go? They were not all volunteers. But the glory of the emperor, that was baloney.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: Oh, my God.

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: I talked your head off.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: Not at all. This was fascinating and amazing stories.

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Yeah. Well, you know, some of this stuff, like I said, I didn't know this was down there. He was big for laminating. He would laminate you if you stood still long enough. But I found this down in the bottom of one drawer. He had two desks full and a file cabinet full and shelves on two walls of this one bedroom and cabinets across here. There was supposed to be a bedroom, but we never could have used it.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: He laminated where he has been and what he has done?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: That's got the whole thing about the history of -- A lot of people don't know. They said, "Farragut, Idaho, for boot camp?"

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: That's where he went?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: That's where he went, yeah. He went there in '42. And we went out there later, and it's made into a state park; and there is markers where each building had been. And there is two buildings left. There is the brig and an office building. So he said, "Let's go in the brig because I have never been in there." We walked in the brig and looked around. He said, "I wasn't in this one; but the other one that had a number over there, that was mine." They had pictures there, the company pictures of all the guys. That was another thing I did. But he said that there that they took those pictures, and he said he couldn't afford to buy one at the time. So she said, "Well, we can have copies made if you find it in the file." And he held it up, and I said, "That's you right on the end. I can tell you anywhere, right there on the end." He said, "Yep, that's me." We bought a picture, and they shipped it us to for fifteen dollars. We got it.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: When you said you worked in a photo lab, what kind of photos would you develop?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: If they would like those that were individual pictures, like in the Navy, we had wedding and the company pictures. The company pictures, they would be on, like, grandstands. And part of my job was, in the fancy uniform we had, I had to carry a big card, like this, with the company number and the date, and I'd stand on this end. The guy had the camera that moved. He would nod. I'd run behind the grandstand over here and get on the end and hold it. So we got in the cutting room with the negative; there is the date and the company number and everything. That's another thing. When we developed the pictures, and then they do this fancy lettering then, you know? But on the end, of course, I am holding up the sign. That was cut off, you know? The cutting room floor was covered with pictures of me all over the place. I have got one. I said, I could have had thousands. I said, I am like the Hollywood stars. My picture was all over the cutting room floor. I held up the thing, you know, okay? He'd nod, and it would go slowly, and I had to run right over to the other end and hold up the sign, okay, so that when he developed it, you got the right company, and the one that does the lettering can put it on the bottom.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: That's so neat. How many times did you have do that?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: Oh, there was a graduation at least once a week. And then the companies, they had to have that ahead of time, so they had to have -- it was quite often because it was a busy, busy time, thousands and thousands of sailors. The guy that worked there, he was from Zion. He had perfected this camera that would move, but stay in focus all the way across, which was quite a deal then, in the forties. So I just held up the sign and run like crazy around to the other. In the summertime, it was outside. In the wintertime, it was in the drill hall. Good thing I didn't ever trip. You had to have it on both ends so they were sure they had the right picture. It was fun, you know? A lot of them from Zion, girls from Zion, were mostly in there because the photographer was from Zion. A lot of stuff laying around, you know? I said, I don't know where everything is. In a hurry, I ran and grabbed what I could find right away. As I said, I can't find my own wedding picture.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: I would have liked to have seen that.

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: I was standing there with that suit on and the orchid corsage.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: What was he wearing?

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: His dress uniform, his dress blues. He was very fussy with clothes. That's why the guys used to borrow them. When he died, I had -- I am not kidding. When I called Salvation Army, I had ten boxes that big of clothes and a bag, that big garbage bag, I had full of socks. I told them, "Bring a truck. Don't come with a van." The guy came in and said, "All this?" I said, "That's full of shoes. That's full of socks. That's full of shirts." He was a clothes horse. His father died when he was six, and his mother didn't have a good education. She came from a family of 12, so she worked in a kitchen somewhere; so he didn't have clothes. And the good-hearted women of the club were so nice to these kids, going to give them clothes. But they wanted everybody to know who gave it to them, so they dyed them purple. Imagine how embarrassing that was for kids to go to school in that purple. He said, "Oh, that purple." He never wanted me to wear purple. But I didn't have anything else to wear. I have got pictures of him when he was a little kid where he had coveralls on. I said, how mean, if you are going to do something nice for a kid and you embarrass them. They had to let everybody know that they were so kind-hearted; they gave them clothes. He said there was three kids in his class, and the other kids would make fun of him, of course. But he lived through it. Clothes horse. So any of this you want to put out there, you are welcome to take. It doesn't make any difference to me.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: Well, let's go ahead and say, okay, so it's 11:15 a.m. So we have had in interview for about an hour and ten minutes, approximately. Thank you so much for sharing your story and sharing your photos and all this information.

sp.speaker: Mary Louise Jensen Giddens
sp.p: And you wore your fingers out.

sp.speaker: Stella Veytsel
sp.p: Thank you very much, Cathleen, for working so hard. (The interview was concluded at 11:15 a.m.)
